facts.text: Grant proposals are a constrained writing genre. Reviewers read against a rubric, in a hurry, under fatigue. A proposal that "reads well" but ignores the funder's stated criteria scores low. A proposal that follows the rubric mechanically but tells a coherent change story scores high.
Three reviewer-tested moves:
Open in the funder's frame. Quote the funding opportunity's priority area in the first two sentences.
Quantify the problem at the right scope. National statistics are weak without local data; local data is weak without national context.
End on the gap. Close with the specific knowledge, service, or capacity gap your project will fill.
"We need money" is a felt need. Demonstrated need is evidence - a quantified disparity, an unmet target, a documented service desert.
Pull from peer-reviewed literature, government data (Census, BLS, CDC, HRSA), and community needs assessments. Avoid undated statistics; reviewers flag anything older than 5 years.

facets.title: 3. Theory of change as the red thread

facts.text: A theory of change is the narrative map of how change happens: if we do X (activities), given Y (assumptions), then Z (outcomes), because of M (mechanism). Reviewers check whether the aims, methods, and evaluation plan trace back to the theory of change.
Critical distinction: outputs are not outcomes. "Conducted 100 workshops" is an output. "Participants reduced X behavior by Y%" is an outcome.
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

Weak: "Improve youth literacy." SMART: "By June 2027, increase the proportion of 4th-grade students at our three partner schools reading at grade level from 42% to 60%, as measured by the state ELA assessment."
One page. Four paragraphs:
Hook + significance. Open with the broad problem. Narrow to the specific gap.
Central hypothesis + rationale. State your hypothesis. Explain why it is plausible. Establish that you are the right team.
Specific Aims. 2-4 aims. Each aim is independent. Use confident verbs: "We will determine," not "We hope to."
Payoff. State the expected outcomes and their impact on the field.
Each cost category (personnel, fringe, travel, equipment, supplies, contractual, indirect) gets a paragraph answering: what, why, how calculated, why this rate.
Reviewer red flags: round numbers without basis, salaries above the federal cap, equipment without quotes.
Strong sustainability plans show:
Diversified funding (other grants secured or pending, earned revenue, in-kind commitments)
Institutionalization (policy adoption, embedded staff lines)
Capacity built (trained personnel, data systems)
Weak: "We will pursue additional funding."

Must contain: the problem, the proposed solution, the requested amount and duration, the lead organization's qualifications, expected outcomes, and the sustainability commitment. Roughly 250-500 words. Write it last.
Every attachment listed in the funding opportunity must be present, named exactly as specified, in the format specified (PDF most often), within the page limit.

> [Funder priority area, quoted or paraphrased from the FOA]. [National-scale statistic with citation, ≤5 years old]. In [target geography], the problem is [more acute] because [local data point]. Despite [existing efforts], [the specific gap]. This proposal addresses [the gap] through [one-sentence approach preview].
Activity list disguised as a proposal. Listing workshops without tying each to an outcome.
Outputs masquerading as outcomes. "We will train 500 people" is not an outcome.
Generic problem statement. Opening with a global statistic with no connection to the funder priority.
Hedge language in aims. "We hope to," "we will attempt to." Use "We will determine."
Sustainability as boilerplate. "We will pursue additional funding."
